claim: Three-methyl cytosine (3meC) are toxic DNA lesions, blocking base pairing.
source: Three-methyl cytosine (3meC) are toxic DNA lesions, blocking base pairing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about 3meC.

claim: Bacteria and humans express members of the AlkB enzymes family, which directly remove 3meC.
source: Bacteria and humans express members of the AlkB enzymes family, which directly remove 3meC.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about AlkB enzymes.

claim: Budding yeast lack the AlkB class of enzymes.
source: However, other organisms, including budding yeast, lack this class of enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about yeast.

claim: The yeast Shu complex is a conserved homologous recombination factor.
source: The yeast Shu complex, a conserved homologous recombination factor, aids in preventing replication-associated mutagenesis from DNA base damaging agents such as methyl methanesulfonate (MMS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of the Shu complex.

claim: The Shu complex aids in preventing replication-associated mutagenesis from DNA base damaging agents such as methyl methanesulfonate (MMS).
source: The yeast Shu complex, a conserved homologous recombination factor, aids in preventing replication-associated mutagenesis from DNA base damaging agents such as methyl methanesulfonate (MMS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior research.

claim: MMS-treated Shu complex-deficient cells exhibit a genome-wide increase in A:T and G:C substitutions mutations.
source: We found that MMS-treated Shu complex-deficient cells exhibit a genome-wide increase in A:T and G:C substitutions mutations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole genome sequencing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The G:C substitutions displayed transcriptional and replicational asymmetries consistent with mutations resulting from 3meC.
source: The G:C substitutions displayed transcriptional and replicational asymmetries consistent with mutations resulting from 3meC.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the strand bias analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Ectopic expression of a human AlkB homolog in Shu-deficient yeast rescues MMS-induced growth defects and increased mutagenesis.
source: Ectopic expression of a human AlkB homolog in Shu-deficient yeast rescues MMS-induced growth defects and increased mutagenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: csm2∆ cells accumulated a median 12.7-fold more mutations than WT upon MMS treatment.
source: Consistent with previous findings, csm2∆ cells accumulated a median 12.7-fold more mutations than WT upon MMS treatment (Figure 1A; Godin et al., 2013; Godin et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with reference to prior studies.

claim: Base substitutions constituted approximately 95% of the total mutations in both the MMS-treated WT and csm2∆ yeast.
source: Base substitutions, insertion/deletion mutations, and complex mutations (consisting of two or more mutations separated by 10 bp or less) were all elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with base substitutions constituting approximately 95% of the total mutations in both the MMS-treated WT and csm2∆ yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MMS-induced mutations were largely randomly distributed across yeast genomes.
source: MMS-induced mutations were largely randomly distributed across yeast genomes (Supplementary file 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 3meA is the most common MMS-induced lesion at A:T base pairs in dsDNA.
source: 3meA is the most common MMS-induced lesion at A:T base pairs in dsDNA and can itself be mutagenic or converted to a mutagenic AP site by the Mag1 glycosylase or by spontaneous depurination (Figure 1B and C; Shrivastav et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior literature.

claim: 3meA can be converted to a mutagenic AP site by the Mag1 glycosylase or by spontaneous depurination.
source: 3meA is the most common MMS-induced lesion at A:T base pairs in dsDNA and can itself be mutagenic or converted to a mutagenic AP site by the Mag1 glycosylase or by spontaneous depurination (Figure 1B and C; Shrivastav et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior literature.

claim: TLS activity on 3meA-derived AP sites leads to an A-> G and A-> T substitution pattern.
source: TLS activity on 3meA-derived AP sites leads to an A-> G and A-> T substitution pattern (Figure 1C) due to the tendency of Rev1 or the replicative polymerase δ incorporating a C or A on AP sites, respectively (Figure 1C; Chan et al., 2013; Haracska et al., 2001; Hoopes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Most substitutions at A:T bases in MMS-treated WT yeast are A to G and A to T.
source: Consequently, most substitutions at A:T bases in MMS-treated WT yeast A to G and A to T (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MMS-treated csm2∆ cells displayed elevated A-> G transitions and A-> T transversions.
source: MMS-treated csm2∆ cells (Figure 1B) displayed elevated A-> G transitions and A-> T transversions, consistent with a function for the Shu complex in the bypass of 3meA or 3meA-derived AP sites, as we recently demonstrated (Godin et al., 2016b; Rosenbaum et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B, with citations to prior work.

claim: 7meG is the most common MMS-induced DNA adduct at G:C base pairs and is not itself mutagenic.
source: 7meG is the most common MMS-induced DNA adduct at G:C base pairs and is not itself mutagenic (Shrivastav et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior literature.

claim: 7meG is eliminated by spontaneous depurination, or Mag1 excision, which both lead to AP sites.
source: However, it is eliminated by spontaneous depurination, or Mag1 excision, which both lead to AP sites (Bjørås et al., 1995; Shrivastav et al., 2010; Wyatt et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior literature.

claim: The MMS-induced mutation profile at G:C base pairs in WT yeast includes high levels of G-> A and G-> C mutations.
source: Interestingly, the MMS-induced mutation profile at G:C base pairs in WT yeast not only includes G-> T mutations but also high levels of G-> A and G-> C mutations (Figure 1D), suggesting that 7meG-derived AP sites are unlikely to cause these mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Deletion of CSM2 results in a similar spectrum of MMS-induced G:C substitutions compared to that observed in WT yeast, but at elevated frequency.
source: Deletion of CSM2 results in a similar spectrum of MMS-induced G:C substitutions compared to that observed in WT yeast, but at elevated frequency, indicating that the Shu complex mediates tolerance of the same MMS-induced lesion that contributes to G:C base pair mutagenesis in WT cells, possibly N3-methylcytosine (3meC).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the data in Figure 1D.

claim: 3meC is a mutagenic DNA adduct predominantly induced by MMS at ssDNA and can block the replicative polymerase.
source: 3meC is a mutagenic DNA adduct predominantly induced by MMS at ssDNA and can block the replicative polymerase (Shrivastav et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior literature.

claim: Rev3-mediated TLS bypass of 3meC leads to the incorporation of a random nucleotide across the lesion.
source: Rev3-mediated TLS bypass of 3meC leads to the incorporation of a random nucleotide across the lesion, leading to a mutational pattern consistent with the one we observed in WT and csm2∆ yeast (Figure 1E; Saini et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2010), indicating that the Shu complex may also bypass this ssDNA-specific alkylation lesion.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: A:T mutations in both MMS-treated WT and csm2Δ yeast showed very little replicative asymmetry, but displayed transcriptional asymmetry.
source: A:T mutations in both MMS-treated WT and csm2Δ yeast showed very little replicative asymmetry, but displayed transcriptional asymmetry, similar to that seen in MMS-treated mag1∆ yeast (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2, with citation to prior work.

claim: G:C mutations in MMS-treated WT yeast displayed little to no transcriptional or replicative strand asymmetry.
source: G:C mutations in MMS-treated WT yeast displayed little to no transcriptional or replicative strand asymmetry, while the same mutations in MMS-exposed csm2∆ cells exhibited both types of strand bias (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: G:C mutations in MMS-exposed csm2∆ cells exhibited both transcriptional and replicative strand bias.
source: G:C mutations in MMS-treated WT yeast displayed little to no transcriptional or replicative strand asymmetry, while the same mutations in MMS-exposed csm2∆ cells exhibited both types of strand bias (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The transcriptional asymmetry displayed higher densities of C mutations on the non-transcribed strand.
source: The transcriptional asymmetry displayed higher densities of C mutations on the non-transcribed strand, consistent with either TC-NER removal of 3meC or preferential formation of 3meCs on the transiently ssDNA non-transcribed strand, instead of an asymmetry derived for TC-NER of 7meG.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Co-deletion of the essential TC-NER factor RAD26 with CSM2 failed to significantly increase MMS-induced CAN1 mutation rates above that of csm2∆ alone.
source: Co-deletion of the essential TC-NER factor RAD26 with CSM2 failed to significantly increase MMS-induced CAN1 mutation rates above that of csm2∆ alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 expression leads to a partial rescue of the growth defects observed in MMS-exposed csm2Δ cells, with ALKBH2 showing a stronger rescue.
source: We find that both ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 expression leads to a partial rescue of the growth defects observed in MMS-exposed csm2Δ cells, with ALKBH2 showing a stronger rescue (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ALKBH2 expression very mildly rescues the MMS sensitivity of WT cells.
source: As expected, ALKBH2 expression very mildly rescues the MMS sensitivity of WT cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The growth defect rescue observed in MMS-treated csm2Δ cells depends on ALKBH2's enzymatic activity.
source: The growth defect rescue observed in MMS-treated csm2Δ cells depends on ALKBH2's enzymatic activity since the expression of an ALKBH2 catalytic dead mutant (ALKBH2-V101R,F120E herein referred to as alkbh2-CD) (Monsen et al., 2010) does not rescue csm2∆ cell viability (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B, with citation to prior work.

claim: ALKBH2 rescues the MMS sensitivity of the other Shu complex members to the same extent.
source: These findings are not specific to csm2∆ as ALKBH2 rescues the MMS sensitivity of the other Shu complex members to the same extent (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The effect of ALKBH2 expression on csm2∆ cell viability is specific for MMS damage.
source: The effect of ALKBH2 expression on csm2∆ cell viability is specific for MMS damage as ALKBH2 expression does not rescue the known growth defect observed in UV-treated csm2Δ rev3Δ double mutant cells (Xu et al., 2013; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D, with citation to prior work.

claim: ALKBH2 expression leads to a dose-dependent increase in the survival of csm2Δ cells acutely exposed to MMS.
source: We observe that ALKBH2 expression leads to a dose-dependent increase in the survival of csm2Δ cells, whereas in WT cells, survival is only mildly rescued (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ALKBH2 rescues the survival phenotype only for cells progressing in the S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: In agreement with our rationale, ALKBH2 was found to rescue the survival phenotype only for cells progressing in the S-phase of the cell cycle, which is when an HR-dependent error tolerance occurs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ALKBH2 expression decreased the mutation rates in MMS-exposed csm2Δ cells.
source: ALKBH2 expression decreased the mutation rates in MMS-exposed csm2Δ cells (Figure 4A; p = 0.0092).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ALKBH2 expression fails to rescue the increase in spontaneous mutations observed in csm2Δ cells.
source: This decreased mutation rate is specific for alkylation lesions as ALKBH2 expression fails to rescue the increase in spontaneous mutations observed in a Shu complex mutant, csm2Δ cells (Figure 4A; p = 0.1327).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rescue of the csm2∆ mutation rate by ALKBH2 depends on ALKBH2 catalytic activity.
source: Furthermore, the rescue of the csm2∆ mutation rate by ALKBH2 depends on ALKBH2 catalytic activity (Figure 4A; p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ALKBH2 expression in csm2Δ cells decreased the frequency of deletions, complex mutations, and substitutions at C:G base pairs.
source: Accordingly, ALKBH2 expression in csm2Δ cells decreased the frequency of deletions, complex mutations, and substitutions at C:G base pairs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Csm2-Psy3 binds to a double-flap substrate containing a 3meC or 1meA lesion on the ssDNA with lower affinity relative to unmodified substrate.
source: While Csm2-Psy3 binds to a double-flap substrate containing a 3meC or 1meA lesion on the ssDNA, it does so with lower affinity relative to unmodified substrate [3meC, Kd = 252 ± 21; 1meA Kd = 313 ± 27; unmodified Kd = 180 ± 29 Figure 4C].
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ALKBH2 expression suppresses the MMS sensitivity of a csm2-F46A mutant to the same extent as a csm2∆ cell.
source: Suggesting that the Shu complex mediator function enables bypass of 3meC, we find that ALKBH2 expression suppresses the MMS sensitivity of a csm2-F46A mutant to the same extent as a csm2∆ cell (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The MMS sensitivity of rad51∆, rad52∆, and rad55∆ is not rescued by ALKBH2 expression to the same extent as the MMS sensitivity of csm2∆ cells.
source: Surprisingly, the MMS sensitivity of rad51∆, rad52∆, and rad55∆ is not rescued by ALKBH2 expression to the same extent as the MMS sensitivity of csm2∆ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: ubc13∆ MMS sensitivity is largely rescued by ALKBH2 expression.
source: In contrast to the Rad51 mediators, ubc13∆ MMS sensitivity is largely rescued by ALKBH2 expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The rad55-S2,8,14A mutant MMS sensitivity is largely rescued by ALKBH2 expression.
source: Unlike rad55∆ cells, the rad55-S2,8,14A mutant MMS sensitivity is largely rescued by ALKBH2 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A csm2∆ rad55-S2,8,14A double mutant exhibits the same MMS sensitivity and mutation rates as a single csm2∆ cell.
source: In contrast, a csm2∆ rad55-S2,8,14A double mutant exhibits the same MMS sensitivity and mutation rates as a single csm2∆ cell (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5E and F.

claim: There is a reduced interaction between Rad55-S2,8,14A with Csm2.
source: Interestingly, we observe a reduced interaction between Rad55-S2,8,14A with Csm2 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 3meC occurs primarily in ssDNA.
source: Among the many alkylation-induced DNA lesions, 3meC is notable for its cytotoxic and mutagenic impact during DNA replication (Nieminuszczy et al., 2009; Shrivastav et al., 2010; Sikora et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: The adduct 3meC is formed endogenously from S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) reactivity with DNA and from the enzymatic activity of DNA methyltransferases.
source: In eukaryotes, the adduct is formed endogenously from S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) reactivity with DNA and from the enzymatic activity of DNA methyltransferases, and exogenously from alkylating agents such as nitrosamines, which are present in the tobacco smoke, temozolomide, or MMS (Chatterjee and Walker, 2017; Dango et al., 2011; Pataillot-Meakin et al., 2016; Rošić et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: Yeast does not encode for an enzyme capable of directly repairing 3meC from ssDNA.
source: Unlike bacteria and higher eukaryotes, yeast does not encode for an enzyme capable of directly repairing 3meC from ssDNA (Admiraal et al., 2019; Sedgwick et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: The Shu complex is primarily involved in the tolerance of replicative base-template damage, being dispensable for DSB repair.
source: The Shu complex is primarily involved in the tolerance of replicative base-template damage, being dispensable for DSB repair (Ball et al., 2009; Godin et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: The Shu complex is an evolutionarily conserved HR factor.
source: The Shu complex is an evolutionarily conserved HR factor that we recently discovered to function in strand-specific DDT during replication and thus provides an excellent model to specifically study HR proteins in the context of PRR (Godin et al., 2015; Godin et al., 2016c; Martino and Bernstein, 2016; Rosenbaum et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the Shu complex is a heterotetramer formed by the SWIM domain-containing protein, Shu2, and the Rad51 paralogs, Csm2, Psy3, and Shu1.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the Shu complex is a heterotetramer formed by the SWIM domain-containing protein, Shu2, and the Rad51 paralogs, Csm2, Psy3, and Shu1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the Shu complex.

claim: The Shu complex promotes Rad51 filament formation, a key step for HR.
source: The Shu complex promotes Rad51 filament formation, a key step for HR (Godin et al., 2016c).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Shu complex mutants are primarily sensitive to the alkylating agent MMS, but not to the DSB-inducing agents such as ionizing radiation.
source: However, this is not the case with the Shu complex, as its mutants are primarily sensitive to the alkylating agent MMS, but not to the DSB-inducing agents such as ionizing radiation (Godin et al., 2016b; Shor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The Shu complex operates in the error-free branch of the PRR to tolerate DNA damage from MMS-induced lesions.
source: Previous studies from our group and others demonstrated that the Shu complex operates in the error-free branch of the PRR to tolerate DNA damage from MMS-induced lesions (Ball et al., 2009; Godin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Cells lacking the BER purinic/apyrimidinic site (AP) endonucleases and AP lyases that process AP sites exhibit exquisite sensitivity toward alkylating agents.
source: Notably, cells lacking the BER purinic/apyrimidinic site (AP) endonucleases and AP lyases that process AP sites exhibit exquisite sensitivity toward alkylating agents and display a three order of magnitude increase in mutations rates when the Shu complex is disrupted.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from prior work.

claim: The Shu complex is important for the tolerance of AP sites.
source: We recently demonstrated that the Shu complex is important for the tolerance of AP sites, also referred to as abasic sites (Rosenbaum et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: In humans, there are nine AlkB homologs with ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 responsible for 3meC DNA repair.
source: In humans, there are nine AlkB homologs with ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 are responsible for 3meC DNA repair (Fedeles et al., 2015; Yi and He, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior literature.

claim: The Shu complex directly functions with the canonical Rad51 paralogs, Rad55-Rad57, and Rad52 to promote HR through Rad51 filament formation.
source: The Shu complex directly functions with the canonical Rad51 paralogs, Rad55-Rad57, and Rad52 to promote HR through Rad51 filament formation (Gaines et al., 2015; Godin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to prior work.

claim: In the context of error-free post-replicative repair, the Shu complex functions downstream of poly-ubiquitination of PCNA by Rad5-Ubc13-Mms2.
source: In the context of error-free post-replicative repair, the Shu complex functions downstream of poly-ubiquitination of PCNA by Rad5-Ubc13-Mms2 (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to prior work.

claim: The Mag1 glycosylase can excise 3meC in dsDNA, therefore, initiating their repair through BER.
source: Recently, the Mag1 glycosylase was shown to excise 3meC in dsDNA, therefore, initiating their repair through BER (Admiraal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: Mag1 cannot excise 3meCs from ssDNA.
source: However, Mag1 cannot excise 3meCs from ssDNA (Admiraal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior literature.

claim: The Shu complex role is functionally conserved in humans and mice.
source: Previous work from our group and others shows that the Shu complex role is functionally conserved in humans and mice (Abreu et al., 2018; Martino and Bernstein, 2016; Martino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Human cells containing Shu complex deletions are sensitive to MMS and DNA alkylating agents.
source: Additionally, human cells containing Shu complex deletions are sensitive to MMS and DNA alkylating agents.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: Both ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 have been proposed as tumor suppressors, being silenced in various tumors, including gastric and breast cancer.
source: This is of particular importance since both ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 have been proposed as tumor suppressors, being silenced in various tumors, including gastric and breast cancer (Fedeles et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2011; Knijnenburg et al., 2018; Stefansson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: ALKBH3 is often overexpressed in different cancers.
source: On the other hand, ALKBH3 is often overexpressed in different cancers and inhibition of ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 can sensitize cancer cells to alkylating chemotherapy (Choi et al., 2011; Koike et al., 2012; Tasaki et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: The upregulation of ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 mediates the resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as temozolomide.
source: Moreover, the upregulation of ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 mediates the resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as temozolomide and ALKBH3 loss leads to endogenous 3meC accumulation in tumors cell lines (Cetica et al., 2009; Dango et al., 2011; Johannessen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: ALKBH3 loss leads to endogenous 3meC accumulation in tumors cell lines.
source: Moreover, the upregulation of ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 mediates the resistance to chemotherapeutic agents such as temozolomide and ALKBH3 loss leads to endogenous 3meC accumulation in tumors cell lines (Cetica et al., 2009; Dango et al., 2011; Johannessen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to prior literature.

claim: The Shu complex may recognize other MMS-induced fork blocking lesions beyond AP sites.
source: However, it remains an outstanding question as to whether the Shu complex may recognize other MMS-induced fork blocking lesions.
evidence: This is implied by the question posed in the introduction, which the study addresses.

claim: The Shu complex helps to mitigate mutations at both A:T and C:G base pairs upon MMS exposure.
source: We determined that the Shu complex prevents mutations at both A:T and C:G base pairs.
evidence: This is inferred from the whole genome sequencing data showing elevated mutations at both base pair types in csm2∆ cells.

claim: The Shu complex has a novel role in the tolerance of three-methyl cytosine (3meC).
source: However, transcriptional and replicative asymmetries in C:G mutations suggest a novel role for the Shu complex in the tolerance of three-methyl cytosine (3meC), in addition to AP sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the strand bias analysis and ALKBH2 rescue experiments.

claim: The ability of the Shu complex to facilitate tolerance of 3meC DNA damage through homology-directed bypass likely highlights an important repair pathway for these lesions even in organisms that express AlkB homologs.
source: Additionally, the ability of the Shu complex to facilitate tolerance of 3meC DNA damage through homology-directly bypass likely highlights an important repair pathway for these lesions even in organisms that express AlkB homologs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The Shu complex functions primarily within the Ubc13-initiated post-replicative repair pathway.
source: This striking result suggests that the Shu complex functions primarily within the Ubc13-initiated post-replicative repair pathway, while the canonical HR genes are also critical for the repair of DSBs induced by MMS through clustered lesions.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the differential rescue by ALKBH2 of ubc13∆ versus other HR mutants.

claim: Deletion of the canonical HR genes leaves cells vulnerable to toxic MMS-induced DSBs formed from lesions that are not subject to ALKBH2 direct reversal.
source: Unlike Shu complex mutant cells, deletion of the canonical HR genes leaves cells vulnerable to toxic MMS-induced DSBs formed from lesions that are not subject to ALKBH2 direct reversal.
evidence: This is stated in the results to explain why canonical HR mutants are not fully rescued by ALKBH2.

claim: Rad55 phosphorylation may stimulate its interaction with Csm2.
source: These results suggest that Rad55 phosphorylation may stimulate its interaction with Csm2 or that Csm2 interacts with Rad55 in that region.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the Y2H data showing reduced interaction between Rad55-S2,8,14A and Csm2.

claim: The Shu complex is likely contributing to the recognition of specific MMS-induced lesions and recruiting the HR machinery to the lesion to facilitate their bypass.
source: In the context of MMS-induced DNA damage, our findings suggest that the Shu complex is likely contributing to the recognition of specific MMS-induced lesions and recruiting the HR machinery, such as Rad55-Rad57, to the lesion to facilitate their bypass and enable their repair following replication.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Mag1 likely plays a significant role in the removal of 3meC from dsDNA after its Shu complex-mediated bypass allows replication to be completed.
source: Mag1 likely plays a significant role in the removal of 3meC from dsDNA after its Shu complex-mediated bypass allows replication to be completed (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 6 as part of the proposed model.

claim: The transcriptional asymmetry of MMS-induced csm2∆ G:C mutations extends up to 167 bp upstream of the transcriptional start site.
source: We additionally note that transcriptional asymmetry of the 3meC in the whole genome sequencing of MMS-treated csm2∆ extends up to 167 bp upstream of the transcriptional start site.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the strand bias analysis.

claim: Replicative asymmetry indicated elevated C mutations associated with the lagging strand template across the yeast genome.
source: Likewise, replicative asymmetry indicated elevated C mutations associated with the lagging strand template across the yeast genome, suggesting that 3meC lesions formed during lagging strand synthesis are bypassed in an error-free manner in Shu proficient yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the replicative strand bias analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The observed strand bias is likely the result of increased formation of 3meC on the non-transcribed strand and not due to the effects of TC-NER.
source: However, this transcriptional asymmetry remained in the spectra of the MMS-treated csm2∆ rad26∆ yeast, suggesting that the observed strand bias is likely the result of increased formation of 3meC on the non-transcribed strand and not due to the effects of TC-NER.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the CAN1 mutation spectra in csm2∆ rad26∆ cells.

claim: The mutation spectrum from mag1∆ csm2Δ double mutant yeast mirrors that from mag1∆ yeast.
source: However, the mutation spectrum from mag1∆ csm2Δ double mutant yeast mirrors that from mag1∆ yeast despite a previously determined higher MMS-induced mutation rate for mag1∆ csm2Δ than mag1-deficient yeast (Godin et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, with citation to prior work.

claim: The elevated frequency of A:T substitutions in mag1∆ csm2Δ yeast compared to csm2Δ yeast is due to higher amounts of 3meA present.
source: This spectrum, therefore, indicates that elevated frequency of A:T substitutions in mag1∆ csm2Δ yeast compared to csm2Δ yeast is due to higher amounts of 3meA present (due to the lack of Mag1) that are normally bypassed with the help of the Shu complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the CAN1 mutation spectra analysis.

claim: tpa1Δ cells show no increased sensitivity to MMS.
source: However, in our hands, and consistent with a recent report (Admiraal et al., 2019), tpa1Δ cells show no increased sensitivity to MMS.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: TPA1 does not exhibit a synthetic sick phenotype with Shu complex mutants upon MMS exposure.
source: Furthermore, unlike other genes that are involved in repairing MMS-induced lesions, we find that TPA1 does not exhibit a synthetic sick phenotype with Shu complex mutants upon MMS exposure (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of MMS-treated mag1∆ yeast contains primarily an elevation of substitutions at A:T base pairs.
